blocks.text: Long, long ago, a wise woman sat all alone under the open sky. She was very old. Giants had brought her up at the very beginning of time, and she remembered everything that had ever happened. She could see things that had not happened yet, too.
One day Odin, the chief of the gods, came to her and looked into her eyes.
"What do you want to ask me?" she said. "Why are you testing me? I know everything, Odin. I even know where you hid your eye, in the deep well of Mimir."
Odin gave her rings and a necklace, and she began to see far and wide, over all the worlds. And she said:
"Be quiet, everyone, great and small, all the children of Heimdall, all the people of the world! Odin wants me to tell the story of the world, the oldest things I can remember.
"I remember the giants, born at the very beginning, who brought me up. I remember nine worlds, and the great tree that grows down under the earth.
"In the beginning there was nothing. There was no sand, and no sea, and no cold waves. There was no earth below, and no sky above. There was only a great yawning gap, and no grass anywhere.
"Then the sons of Bor lifted up the earth, and they made Midgard, the middle world, where people live. The sun shone from the south onto the stones, and the ground grew green with grass.

"But the sun did not know where her home was. The moon did not know how strong he was. And the stars did not know where they belonged. So the gods sat down together on their thrones, and they gave names to the night and to the new moon. They named the morning and the middle of the day, the afternoon and the evening, so that people could count the years.

"The gods met on the Plain of Ida. They built tall temples, and they built forges, and they made treasures, and tongs, and tools. They played board games together, and they were happy, and they had all the gold they wanted. Until three powerful giant maidens came out of Giantland.

"Then the gods made the dwarves. Motsognir was the greatest of them, and Durin was next. They made many dwarves out of the earth, shaped like people. Their names were Nori and Bombur, Thorin and Thror, Fili and Kili, Dvalin and Gandalf, and Eikinskialdi, which means Oakenshield, and many, many more.

"Then three gods, strong and kind, came walking through the world. On the land they found Ask and Embla, who could do almost nothing, and had no future at all. They had no breath, and no thoughts, no blood, no movement and no healthy color. Odin gave them breath. Hoenir gave them thoughts. And Lodur gave them blood and healthy color. And so they became the first people. (Another old story says it was Odin and his two brothers who did this, but this is how the wise woman told it.)

"I know an ash tree that stands there. Its name is Yggdrasil. It is very tall, and it is washed with shining white water. From it comes the dew that falls into the valleys. It stands forever green over the Well of Urd.

"From there come three wise maidens, from the hall under that tree. One is called Urd, the second is Verdandi, and the third is Skuld. They carve on pieces of wood. They make the laws, and they choose the lives of all the children of people, and they say what will happen to them.
"I saw the Valkyries coming from far away, ready to ride: Skuld with a shield, and Skogul, Gunn, Hild, Gondul and Geirskogul. Those are Odin's warrior maidens, ready to ride over the earth.

"I remember the first war in the world. A woman named Gullveig came to the gods, a woman of magic. The gods tried to get rid of her with spears and with fire, three times. But three times she was born again, and she is still alive. Then the Vanir, the other family of gods, came marching across the plains, and they broke down the wall around the gods' home. Odin threw his spear over the army. That was the first war in the world.

"I remember when the gods asked one another who had promised Freyja to a giant. Thor was so angry that he could not sit still, and he broke the promise. After that, oaths and promises were not kept any more. (Another story tells about that giant, who built the gods' wall.)
"I know that Heimdall's horn is hidden under the holy tree. And I see a waterfall pouring from the place where Odin left his eye. Do you know enough yet? Or shall I go on?

"Far in the east, in the Iron Wood, an old giantess sat and raised the children of the wolf Fenrir. One of them will swallow the moon one day. Then the sunshine will turn dark for many summers, and all the weather will turn to storms. Do you know enough yet? Or shall I go on?

"A giant sat on a hill, playing his harp. He was glad Eggther, the giantess's watchman. Near him in the woods, a bright red rooster named Fjalar crowed. Over the gods crowed another rooster, Goldcomb, who wakes the heroes in Odin's hall. And a third rooster, sooty red, crows under the earth in the halls of Hel.

"I saw what would happen to Baldur, Odin's son. High on the plain grew a little plant, slender and very fair. It was the mistletoe. From it a dart was made, and Hodur threw it. And Frigg wept in her hall for the sorrow of Valhalla. Do you know enough yet? Or shall I go on?
"I saw someone lying tied up, under the grove of the hot springs. He looked like Loki. And there sits Sigyn, his wife, beside him, and she is not glad. Do you know enough yet? Or shall I go on?

"I saw a golden hall in the north, on the Dark Fells, for the family of the dwarf Sindri. And I saw a hall far from the sun, on the Shore of the Dead, with its doors facing north. Its walls are woven from the backs of snakes, and poison drips in through the roof. In the cold, slow rivers there, I saw people wading who had told lies and done terrible things. That is where the dragon Nidhogg lives. Do you know enough yet? Or shall I go on?
"Now I see further. I can tell much about Ragnarok, the doom of the gods.

"Brothers will fight each other, and families will turn against each other. It will be a hard world, a time of axes, a time of swords, a time of winds, a time of wolves, before the world falls. No one will spare anyone.

"Heimdall will raise his horn and blow it loudly. Odin will speak with Mimir's head. The great ash tree Yggdrasil will tremble and groan, and Loki will get free. In front of his cave, the hound Garm will howl and break his chain, and the wolf will run.

"The giant Hrym will come steering from the east. The sea will rise. The Midgard Serpent will twist in rage and beat the water, and the eagle will scream. A ship will come over the sea from the east, full of the people of fire, and Loki will steer it. And all the monsters will go with the wolf.
"Surt will come from the south with flickering fire, and his sword will shine like the sun. The rocky hills will crash together, and the sky will split open.
"Then Odin will go out to fight the wolf, and Frey will fight Surt. And Odin will fall. That will be Frigg's second sorrow.
"Then Odin's son Vidar will come to fight the wolf, and he will drive his sword into its heart, and so pay it back for his father.
"Then Thor will come, the son of the Earth, and in his anger he will kill the Midgard Serpent. Then he will walk nine steps away from the serpent, and fall.
"The sun will turn black. The earth will sink into the sea. The bright stars will fall from the sky. Smoke and fire will rage around the great tree, and the flames will leap up to the sky itself.
"But I see the earth rise up a second time out of the sea, green and lovely. Waterfalls tumble down, and an eagle flies over them, catching fish in the mountain streams.

"The gods meet again on the Plain of Ida. They talk about the Midgard Serpent, and they remember all the great things that happened long ago. And there in the grass they find again the wonderful golden game pieces that the gods played with in the old days.

"Fields will grow without anyone sowing them. Everything bad will be made better. Baldur will come back, and Baldur and Hodur will live together in Odin's halls. And I see a hall standing, brighter than the sun, roofed with gold, at a place called Gimle. Good people will live there, and be happy forever."
Then, far away, the wise woman saw the dark dragon Nidhogg come flying up from the deep, over the plains. And then she sank down, and she said no more.

A simplified retelling of “The Vala's Prophecy” in The Elder Edda, translated by Benjamin Thorpe (1866). The original is listed under Other versions. Thorpe calls the wise woman a “Vala” and spells the names “Baldr” and “Hödr.”
